name: eWo Championship
epitaph: The promotion's own top prize, and the belt that opened it: "The Idol" Bill Dynamite beat "The Dealer" Dylan Dunn two falls to one at eWo's first pay-per-view in September 2004, in a tournament final refereed by Erin Jacobs, and the fed's own history calls that night the true start of its success. Dunn is separately recorded as an eWo World Heavyweight Champion, on the same Hall of Fame page. The belt came back with the promotion: Cody Clark pulled it out of a briefcase at BWF Danger Zone 2007 and handed it to The Legend, who put down the BWF Championship to take it. Legend lost it to Czecher in a four-way at Hell & Back, regained it from Czecher at Body Count with a new finisher, then defended it through Supremacy, License to Thrill and Guilty As Charged before Frank Murdoch became the first man ever to pin him in eWo, at The New Black — the reign eWo closed on, in November 2007, with no further word. C.M. Vyrus was reigning by the 2008 return's own sixth of April; Kyle Cross was carrying it into a barbed-wire main event at the record's own last word.
notes: The fed's own Hall of Fame page lists "eWo Champion" and "eWo World Heavyweight Champion" as separate lines for separate men. Whether those are one lineage under two names or two belts is not settled anywhere in the surviving record, and both readings are left standing.

name: eWo Primetime Championship
epitaph: A championship that outlived three of the promotions that carried it. It began in eWo when Johnny Legend won a ladder match at Bound for Glory, and passed through Gabe Shelley, Lawrence Jarvis and Seth Thomas before the promotion closed in December 2004 with nobody left to compete for it. Shelley, its last eWo champion, took it to the Blazenwing Wrestling Federation, which bought the rights to it outright and defended it until spring 2006; px:w's chairman Paul Reynolds then purchased it and activated it there; when px:w closed it went back to BWF for a short while. In the fed's own words it "is one of a select few championships that has gone through many federations," and "many believe it lost it's prestige and it has since been abandoned."

name: eWo United States Championship
epitaph: eWo's secondary singles belt, defended twice a month under the fed's own rules. Czecher held it in the promotion's first run. In its second, Cody Clark carried it into BWF Danger Zone 2007 in a briefcase and handed it to Chris Roman in the middle of the ring; Roman held it up for the crowd to read, then laid it down and walked out with the rest of them.

name: eWo Tag-Team Championship
epitaph: The promotion's tag titles, defended once a month. Bill Dynamite and Czecher held them in the first run, Dylan Dunn and Scott Royal twice; AJ Donavon and Bobby Dynamite, Xaria Linette and Alexis Sykes, and C.M. Vyrus and Ryley Wynters as Nuclear Wynter all held them afterwards. The Takeover were defending them on the 11 November 2007 card, and Nuclear Wynter had them back by April 2008 — with a shirt of their own in the fed's own store. The Iconoclast were the champions by the Hell and Back card, billed against the former champions The Takeover.

name: eWo National Championship
epitaph: A first-run championship whose only recorded holder is its first: Lawrence Jarvis, on the promotion's own Hall of Fame page. No later reign appears anywhere in the surviving record.

name: eWo Gutz & Glory Championship
epitaph: A first-run championship recorded once, on Czecher, in the promotion's own Hall of Fame. What it was contested for, and who else held it, is not in the surviving record.

name: eWo Triple Crown Championship
epitaph: Recorded once in the promotion's own Hall of Fame, on Czecher, listed alongside — not instead of — his eWo, United States, Gutz & Glory and Tag Team reigns. Whether it was a physical belt or the fed's own name for holding the other three is not settled in the surviving record.

name: eWo Valor Championship
epitaph: A second-run singles belt, and the busiest one in the fed's own rulebook: three defences every month, more than any other championship it carried. AJ Donavon and Ryley Wynters both held it.

name: eWo Television Championship
epitaph: Defended every week under the fed's own rules — the fastest clock any eWo belt ran on. Ryley Wynters was its first champion; Nijs Landzaat took it after ending Erin Jacobs' winning streak, and the fed's own account has his manager pushing for a bigger contract on the strength of it and being turned down.

name: eWo Commonwealth Championship
epitaph: Introduced in the promotion's Toronto era and first held by Reno Drake. Ryley Wynters was carrying it into a triple threat against Paul Herring and Juan Ramirez on the 20 April 2008 card; the results page for that show was never captured. By the 18 May 2008 card Erik Dafoe was the champion, and he was billed to defend it against Juan Ramirez at Hell and Back.

name: eWo Freedom Championship
epitaph: The last championship eWo created, first held by Jack Darling. The surviving record shows it fought over in two table matches — an Elimination Tables Match at The Crowning: Epic Homecoming on 23 March 2008, and an Ultimate Tables Match three weeks later where Nijs Landzaat defended it against Nick Toretto — neither with a result that survives. By May 2008 Eryk Adams was the champion, billed to defend it against Eden Turner at Hell and Back.

name: AJ Epic Memorial Cup
epitaph: A tournament named for the promotion's own founder after the fed staged his death, and run twice. The first, in 2006, was hosted by px:w rather than by eWo, which was closed at the time; Reno Drake won it at High Impact in August of that year and took a px:w World Championship match out of it, losing to Cody Clark. The second went to Scott Free, a newcomer, in the promotion's own 2007 run. eWo's own titles page claims both.
